name: acl2
desc: Logic and programming language in which you can model computer systems
why: A Lisp-based theorem prover used to model and formally verify real hardware and systems, a genuinely deep rabbit hole.

brief.what_it_is: ACL2 is a logic and programming language, built on a dialect of Common Lisp, in which you write models of computer systems and then use an accompanying theorem-proving tool to prove properties about those models. The homepage describes it as "A Computational Logic for Applicative Common Lisp" and places it in the Boyer-Moore family of provers. The input is ACL2 definitions and theorems, typically organised into files called books, and the output is machine-checked proofs or failed proof attempts. The page is for Version 8.7, dated March 20, 2026.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a way to model computer systems and prove properties of those models, and it credits the Boyer-Moore provers with the 2005 ACM Software System Award. It also points to a large shared library of community books so users can reuse existing definitions and lemmas.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internal proof machinery. It does describe the usage model: you write definitions and theorems, collect them into books, and can certify and reuse community books that others have written. Extensions include ACL2(r) for real numbers via non-standard analysis, ACL2(p) for parallel evaluation, and the Eclipse-based ACL2 Sedan (ACL2s), which adds termination-proof automation and counterexample generation.

commands_seen.context: Shown on the homepage as the first step for building the ACL2+Books manual locally from the source distribution.

Builds the ACL2+Books manual locally; the placeholder is the path to your ACL2 executable. The page says it uses ccl by default and that sbcl is also acceptable, and that it may take several minutes or longer depending on which books are already certified.
Referenced as the ACL2 terminal command for reading documentation, as in 'the ACL2 :DOC command at the terminal'. Mentioned in prose, not shown as a standalone command line.

brief.install_notes: The homepage links to an 'Obtaining, Installing, and License' page, which I did not fetch. Community books are downloaded and installed separately, per the installation instructions. Building the full manual from source requires a local ACL2 binary and, by default, Clozure Common Lisp (ccl), with SBCL also acceptable. ACL2s is distributed separately by Pete Manolios's group and ships a standard executable ACL2 image for Windows. The brew executables are listed as acl2 and acl2p, where acl2p is the parallel-evaluation build.
brief.standout: It is a theorem prover where the models are written in an executable Lisp dialect, so the same artefact can be run and proved, and it has a large community library of reusable proven books. The homepage's own emphasis is that the manual and books are at least as large as the system itself.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as the homepage shows: it is on Version 8.7 with the page dated March 20, 2026, and the authors and community maintain books and documentation. I did not check a repository commit date or release history.
brief.caveats: The homepage does not describe hardware or systems verification. The scout note's claim that it is used to model and verify real hardware and systems is not supported by the text I read, though that is a known use. The homepage warns newcomers not to wander into the full manual and to start with the START-HERE topic. Building the manual is slow. ACL2s, the Eclipse-based variant, is distributed by a different group and is not the same as the base ACL2 executable.
quotes: ACL2 is a logic and programming language in which you can model computer systems, together with a tool to help you prove properties of those models.
If you are a newcomer to ACL2, we do not recommend that you wander off into the full documentation.
ACL2 is freely available under the terms of the LICENSE file distributed with ACL2.
